title: AFR Property Summit 2026: RBA sees housing slump but no 'recession'
full_text:
Reserve Bank of Australia assistant governor Sarah Hunter says a slump in the housing market is hurting the broader economy and will dampen the construction of new homes, but rejected developers' claims that it was pushing the country into recession.
Despite the housing slowdown, Hunter told The Australian Financial Review Property Summit that the RBA board could increase interest rates when it meets later this month, given persistent cost increases.
"We are concerned about inflation, and if there is a sense that inflation is going to be stronger than we think in the context of our forecast, then the board may well have to raise interest rates to tackle that," she said.
The central bank's preferred underlying inflation measure, which strips out volatile price changes, was stuck at 3.6 per cent over the 12 months to July, above the bank's target of between 2 per cent and 3 per cent. RBA governor Michele Bullock warned last month that the bank would lift interest rates if there were "upside risks" to inflation, and bond traders are pricing in about a 70 per cent chance of a rate rise on September 29.
The housing downturn - which wiped more than $34 billion off the value of dwellings in the three months to June 30, according to figures published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Tuesday - is reverberating across the economy, hurting consumer sentiment and squeezing construction margins even further.
The property market began to cool when the RBA started raising interest rates earlier this year. The downturn intensified after Labor's May budget axed negative gearing and the 50 per cent discount on capital gains, except for new homes.
Hunter said the decline in housing turnover had already affected real estate agents, conveyancing lawyers and removalists.
The continued decline in home values would make people feel less wealthy and spend less on furniture and new cars, but the overall reduction in consumer spending was likely to be "relatively small", she said. Housing construction would fall in 2027 and 2028.
"So it's definitely going to slow things down," Hunter said. "Given everything else that's going on, then we wouldn't expect right now to see a recession or anything like that in the economy."
The average national dwelling price fell 0.7 per cent to $1.1 million in the June quarter. NSW (-2.4 per cent) and Victoria (-2.1 per cent) recorded their biggest price falls since the last housing downturn, which occurred between 2017 and 2019 amid the banking royal commission, and when regulators tightened bank lending rules.
Property analysts are tipping that national prices will fall about 10 per cent from peak to trough, with outsized declines expected in the interest rate-sensitive market of Sydney.
Nigel Satterley, one of Australia's largest private property developers, warned the housing downturn was very serious and the nation was facing a "full-blown recession" unless the government reversed its changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax.
The swift decline in prices and slump in housing turnover would flow through to spending at retailers and shopping malls, he said.
"The government's going to realise housing is a huge, huge multiplier," Satterley told the summit. "If we don't [U-turn], then Australia goes into a period of high unemployment and a deep retail or housing-led recession."
Sydney auctioneer Damien Cooley said there was now an average of 2.1 bidders per home, down from seven bidders in a boom market.
Domain chief economist Nicola Powell said housing was almost 70 per cent of household wealth, so a decline in house prices would slow consumer spending. "That's a good thing for inflation, though. We need inflation to come down. I'm concerned probably more around the new [housing] supply effects and how it's going to have a negative impact on that over that longer term."
ANZ chief economist Richard Yetsenga said household balance sheets were "very, very strong" and mortgage defaults were below 1 per cent, even with mortgage rates at a 15-year high.
"We are probably going through quite a substantial change in the housing market, and one that probably needed to happen, and we've done it before," he said. "We can't keep growing house prices to income and think that everything will be fine."
Morgan Stanley chief economist Chris Read said the changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax were responsible for perhaps half of the forecast 10 per cent decline in national house prices.
Consumer spending and housing construction would slow, but household balance sheets were strong enough to ride out the downturn, he said.
"The prospect of sort of widespread household stress, at least in terms of house values, is lower than it has been in prior downturns," Read said. "But I think what we're seeing in the housing market suggests that the slowdown is only going to broaden from here."
The Albanese government has come under fire from the property industry and federal opposition for imposing tax changes that have reduced the value of Australians' biggest asset and could crimp the supply of new homes.
Federal Housing Minister Clare O'Neil told the summit the tax changes were putting first home buyers on a "level playing field" with investors. "Perhaps this is maybe controversial in this room, but I think if we fast-forward three or four years, we are going to wonder how we left it so long that the young people of this country are being taxed to subsidise investors to buy a second, third, fifth, sixth property, when they're unable to get into a position to buy their first home."
O'Neil said Treasury's forecast for the tax changes to cause house prices to grow by 2 per cent less over two years was in line with the Commonwealth Bank (-5 per cent) and the Grattan Institute. The 10-15 per cent price peak-to-trough fall some analysts are now forecasting was mainly due to interest rates, she said.
